content:
With the recent formalization of FLT by antropic. I think it is clear that we are now living in a world where the creation of formalizations is easy. I just wanted to make it clear how I see the future of projects like Physlib in this world.

I think to see this, it is worth looking at other languages like python. Here code has been plentiful for a very long time. Yet 'standard libraries' such as scipy, numpy etc. still exist, and I suspect will continue to do so. The reason is, that even in a world where the code itself is plentiful it is still worthwhile having libraries with the best quality of code possible, which is trusted and inter-compatible. I see projects like Mathlib, Physlib and CSLib, filling this role.

I think what this means for us, is that we need to continue to make sure that the quality of code in Physlib is to the best standard as possible. Learning from the other formalizations that happen in and around this area.
A high quality library is alwasy needed so that when people/ai is trying to start on a project they do not need to reinvent all the wheels. It is valid even when AI can generate high quality code.

Humans still need to check theorem statements and the definitions they refer to before trusting an autoformalized proof. While this burden is relatively negligible for problems like FLT, which are orders of magnitude easier to state than to prove, the gap may be much smaller in applied physics. In that case, the quality, composability, and faithfulness to first principles of core definitions and interfaces may matter more than the elegance of the proofs built on top of them.
